listenings.text: I give my students a one-month plan. In week one, they keep the original audio and switch the subtitles to English. That's all. In week two, they rewatch something they already know very well. A cartoon, a favorite film. Because they know the plot, they can stop worrying about the story and listen to the language. And in weeks three and four, they turn the subtitles off for ten minutes a day. Most of them tell me they feel exhausted at first. Their eyes and ears are working together for the first time. I tell them it's completely normal, and that it gets easier after a week or two. And it always does.

People ask me what I do, and I say I write the words at the bottom of the screen. But there's a difference between subtitles and closed captions. Subtitles show what people say. Closed captions also describe the sounds. Door slams. Music playing. Someone laughing in another room. Captions were first made for people who are deaf or hard of hearing, and that's still the main reason they exist. But today lots of other people use them. Modern films have a lot of background noise, the dialogue is fast, the accents are different. Even my mum, who's never had a problem with her hearing, watches everything with captions on now.

My kids are learning Spanish, and my secret weapon is cartoons. But not new ones. I take the cartoons they already know and love in English, and I switch the audio to Spanish. At first they complained. Now they don't even notice. Why does it work? Because they already know the story. They know what happens next, so they're not stressed about the plot, and they pay attention to the words. And they rewatch the same episodes again and again, which is exactly what you need to pick up a language. Last month, my son used a Spanish expression from his favorite cartoon in a real conversation with our neighbor. I couldn't believe it.

reading.rtitle: Subtitles On, Language Off? Three Steps to Better Listening
paras: In some countries, almost everything on TV is dubbed. In others, foreign movies keep their original voices and come with subtitles. Teachers often point out that people in the second group seem to pick up English more easily, and it makes sense: they hear real English every day, at real speed. But if you read subtitles in your own language, how much English are you really listening to? Not as much as you think. Your eyes do most of the work, and your ears relax.

Many teachers suggest a simple plan in three steps. Step one: keep the original audio, and try switching the subtitles to English. It feels slower at first, but now your eyes and ears get the same words, and you start to catch expressions you used to miss. Step two: rewatch something you already know, like a cartoon from your childhood or a movie you love. You know the plot, so your brain can stop worrying about the story and focus on the language. Step three: turn the subtitles off for a few minutes a day, and try to get the gist without help.

Do not expect to keep up with every word, especially in scenes with a lot of background noise. Even native speakers turn on closed captions more and more. And do not feel guilty if you binge-watch a series with a great cliffhanger at the end of every episode. If it keeps you watching in English, it is doing its job. The important thing is to remember to choose English, every time you press play.
